_note: Execution tags (annotations) label individual workflow RUNS — not the workflow definition itself. Users tag executions during post-execution review to classify outcomes.

_difference_from_workflow_tags.workflow_tags: Categorize the workflow DEFINITION ('Production', 'Sales', 'Billing'). Applied once, describe the workflow's identity.
_difference_from_workflow_tags.execution_tags: Categorize individual RUNS of a workflow ('needs-review', 'false-positive', 'customer-escalation', 'data-quality-issue'). Applied per execution, describe what happened in that specific run.

_llm_can_infer: Execution tag names reveal HOW the team triages and classifies operational incidents
Tags like 'false-positive' show the team actively reviews and filters automation outputs
Tags like 'customer-escalation' show automations directly impact customer experience
Tag frequency across executions reveals recurring operational patterns
Presence of execution tags at all = mature ops team that reviews automation outcomes
ABSENCE of execution tags = team doesn't review runs (governance gap signal)

_business_value.operational_maturity: If a team tags executions, they review automation outcomes. This is a strong maturity signal — most teams don't do this.
_business_value.incident_classification: Tag names reveal the team's mental model for problems. 'data-quality-issue' vs 'timeout' vs 'customer-impact' shows what they care about.
_business_value.pattern_detection: If 30% of executions for one workflow are tagged 'needs-review', that workflow has reliability issues the team is manually compensating for. Expliq should surface this.
_business_value.governance_signal: Execution tags per workflow = active governance. No tags = nobody is checking outputs. This directly feeds the risk engine.
_business_value.recommendation_fuel: Many 'false-positive' tags → recommend better filtering logic. Many 'timeout' tags → recommend retry/timeout configuration. The tags TELL us what to recommend.

_priority_for_demo: Medium-low. Depends on whether fairtix instance has execution tags. If it does, it's a nice insight. If not, skip gracefully.
